questiontext.text: A path in a graph is a simple path when:

answer.text: No node appears more than once, except that the first and last node may be identical

feedback.text: Correct — a simple path has no internal repeats; only the endpoints may coincide (a round trip).

answer.text: It visits every node of the graph exactly once

feedback.text: That is a Hamiltonian path; a simple path need not touch every node.

answer.text: It runs from an initial node to a final node

feedback.text: That is a test path / complete path; a simple path can start and end anywhere.

answer.text: No edge is traversed more than once

feedback.text: Simplicity is defined on nodes, not edges; a simple path forbids repeated nodes (except the endpoints).

generalfeedback.text: A simple path repeats no node, with the single exception that its first and last node may be the same, which lets a simple path form a loop (a round trip).

questiontext.text: A prime path is:

answer.text: A simple path that is not a proper subpath of any other simple path (a maximal simple path)

feedback.text: Correct — a prime path is a simple path that cannot be extended into a longer simple path.

answer.text: The shortest path between two nodes

feedback.text: Prime paths are about maximality of simple paths, not shortest distance.

answer.text: Any path from the initial node to a final node

feedback.text: That is a complete/test path; a prime path need not start at entry or end at exit.

answer.text: A path that visits every node exactly once

feedback.text: That is a Hamiltonian path; a prime path need not visit every node.

generalfeedback.text: A prime path is a maximal simple path: it is simple, and no longer simple path contains it as a contiguous subpath.

questiontext.text: An edge-pair is:

answer.text: A path of length 2 — two consecutive edges u→v→w sharing the middle node v

feedback.text: Correct — an edge-pair is a length-2 path formed by two adjacent edges.

answer.text: Any two edges of the graph, whether or not they are adjacent

feedback.text: An edge-pair requires the two edges to be adjacent (share a middle node), forming a length-2 path.

answer.text: A single edge together with its reverse

feedback.text: Direction is not reversed; an edge-pair is two consecutive forward edges.

answer.text: A pair of nodes connected by an edge

feedback.text: That is just an edge; an edge-pair is two adjacent edges (a length-2 path).

generalfeedback.text: An edge-pair is a path of length 2: edges u→v and v→w chained through a shared middle node v.

questiontext.text: A complete path in a control-flow graph is:

answer.text: A path that starts at an initial node and ends at a final node

feedback.text: Correct — a complete path runs the whole way from entry to exit.

answer.text: A simple path that cannot be extended

feedback.text: That is a prime path; a complete path is defined by its entry/exit endpoints and may repeat nodes.

answer.text: A path that visits every edge of the graph

feedback.text: Covering every edge is Edge Coverage; a complete path just runs from entry to exit.

answer.text: Any path of length 2

feedback.text: That is an edge-pair, not a complete path.

generalfeedback.text: A complete path goes from an initial node to a final node; each program execution follows one complete path, and it may repeat nodes (e.g. loop iterations).

questiontext.text: In graph-based testing, a test path is:

answer.text: A path that starts at an initial node and ends at a final node — one complete execution

feedback.text: Correct — a test path represents one run of the program from entry to exit.

answer.text: A simple path that is maximal

feedback.text: That is a prime path; a test path may repeat nodes and must run entry to exit.

answer.text: Any single edge of the graph

feedback.text: A single edge is a length-1 path, not necessarily a full entry-to-exit execution.

answer.text: A path that never repeats a node

feedback.text: Test paths may repeat nodes (loops); only simple paths forbid internal repeats.

generalfeedback.text: A test path runs from an initial node to a final node; a test case executes exactly one test path, which may traverse loops and repeat nodes.

questiontext.text: A round-trip path is:

answer.text: A prime path of nonzero length whose first and last node are the same

feedback.text: Correct — a round-trip path is a prime path that begins and ends at the same node.

answer.text: Any path from the initial node to a final node and back

feedback.text: A round-trip path is a maximal simple cycle (prime), not a full entry-exit-entry run.

answer.text: A path that traverses every edge in both directions

feedback.text: Round-trip refers to returning to the starting node, not to reversing edges.

answer.text: A path of length 2

feedback.text: That is an edge-pair; a round-trip path is a prime path with coinciding endpoints.

generalfeedback.text: A round-trip path is a prime path (a maximal simple path) whose first and last nodes coincide, i.e. a simple cycle that cannot be extended.

questiontext.text: Prime Path Coverage (PPC) is satisfied when:

answer.text: Every prime path of the graph is toured by at least one test path

feedback.text: Correct — PPC requires each prime path to be toured.

answer.text: Every edge of the graph is traversed

feedback.text: That is Edge Coverage, which PPC subsumes but is weaker than PPC.

answer.text: Every complete path is executed

feedback.text: That is Complete Path Coverage, which is stronger and usually infeasible.

answer.text: Every node is visited

feedback.text: That is Node Coverage, the weakest of these criteria.

generalfeedback.text: Prime Path Coverage imposes one test requirement per prime path: each prime path must be toured by some test path.

questiontext.text: Edge-Pair Coverage (EPC) is satisfied when the test paths tour:

answer.text: Every reachable path of length up to 2 (each edge-pair, plus edges/nodes that cannot be extended)

feedback.text: Correct — EPC requires every reachable path of length ≤ 2.

answer.text: Every reachable edge, and nothing more

feedback.text: That is Edge Coverage; EPC additionally requires the adjacent edge-pairs.

answer.text: Every prime path of the graph

feedback.text: That is Prime Path Coverage, which is stronger than EPC.

answer.text: Every complete path from entry to exit

feedback.text: That is Complete Path Coverage, far stronger and usually infeasible.

generalfeedback.text: Edge-Pair Coverage requires every reachable path of length ≤ 2; the length-2 paths are the edge-pairs, and shorter paths are included for elements that cannot be extended.

questiontext.text: Complete Path Coverage (CPC) is satisfied when:

answer.text: Every complete path (from an initial node to a final node) is executed by some test path

feedback.text: Correct — CPC requires all complete paths, which is why loops usually make it infeasible.

answer.text: Every prime path is toured

feedback.text: That is Prime Path Coverage, which is weaker than CPC.

answer.text: Every edge-pair is toured

feedback.text: That is Edge-Pair Coverage, much weaker than CPC.

answer.text: Every node is visited at least once

feedback.text: That is Node Coverage, the weakest criterion here.

generalfeedback.text: Complete Path Coverage requires touring every complete path; with a loop there are infinitely many complete paths, so CPC is generally infeasible.

name.text: Identify a prime path in a diamond

questiontext.text: A CFG has edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 3→4 (node 1 initial, node 4 final). Which of the following is a prime path?

feedback.text: Correct — 1→2→4 is a maximal simple path; it cannot be extended at either end.
2→4 is a proper subpath of 1→2→4, so it is not maximal and not prime.
1→2 is a proper subpath of 1→2→4, so it is not prime.
There is no edge 3→2, so this is not even a valid path.

generalfeedback.text: The prime paths of this diamond are 1→2→4 and 1→3→4; each is a maximal simple path, while 2→4 and 1→2 are proper subpaths and 1→3→2 is not a path at all.

questiontext.text: A CFG has edges 1→2, 2→3, 1→3. How many edge-pairs (length-2 paths u→v→w) does it have?

feedback.text: Correct — only 1→2→3 chains two adjacent edges; 1→3 and 2→3 have no continuation.
Only one length-2 path exists (1→2→3); node 3 has no outgoing edge to continue.
Three is the edge count; edge-pairs count adjacent edge chains, of which there is only one.
1→2 followed by 2→3 forms the edge-pair 1→2→3, so the count is 1, not 0.

generalfeedback.text: For each edge u→v look for an edge v→w: only 1→2 (v=2) continues via 2→3, giving the single edge-pair 1→2→3.

questiontext.text: A CFG has edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 3→4. How many edge-pairs (length-2 paths u→v→w) does it have?

feedback.text: Correct — 1→2→4 and 1→3→4 are the only length-2 chains.
Four is the edge count; only two adjacent edge chains exist (1→2→4, 1→3→4).
Recount — the chains are 1→2→4 and 1→3→4, so there are two.
Both 1→2→4 and 1→3→4 are edge-pairs, so the count is two.

generalfeedback.text: Edge-pairs: 1→2 continues via 2→4 (1→2→4), and 1→3 continues via 3→4 (1→3→4); edges into node 4 have no continuation, so the total is 2.

questiontext.text: How many edges does an edge-pair (a path of length 2) contain, and how many nodes does it visit?

answer.text: 2 edges and 3 nodes (u, v, w)

feedback.text: Correct — two consecutive edges u→v and v→w span three nodes.

answer.text: 1 edge and 2 nodes

feedback.text: That is a single edge (length 1), not an edge-pair.

answer.text: 2 edges and 2 nodes

feedback.text: Two distinct consecutive edges span three nodes, not two.

answer.text: 3 edges and 4 nodes

feedback.text: That is a path of length 3; an edge-pair has length 2.

generalfeedback.text: Path length counts edges: a length-2 path has 2 edges (u→v, v→w) and therefore visits 3 nodes.

name.text: Which sequence is a simple path

questiontext.text: Ignoring which edges exist, which of the following node sequences is a simple path?

feedback.text: Correct — all four nodes are distinct, so it is simple.
Node 2 repeats in an internal position (not as first=last), so it is not simple.
Node 2 repeats consecutively in the middle, so it is not simple.
Node 3 repeats internally (positions 2 and 4), so it is not simple.

generalfeedback.text: A simple path forbids any repeated node except a possible first=last coincidence; 1→2→3→4 has all distinct nodes, while the others repeat a node internally.

questiontext.text: Complete Path Coverage is usually infeasible when the program under test contains a loop.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — a loop yields infinitely many complete paths (one per iteration count), so CPC cannot generally be achieved.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: A loop lets the number of complete paths grow without bound, so touring all of them is infeasible.

generalfeedback.text: Each additional loop iteration is a distinct complete path, so a loop produces infinitely many complete paths and CPC becomes infeasible.

questiontext.text: A CFG has edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 3→4, 4→5, 4→6 (node 1 initial; nodes 5 and 6 final). How many prime paths does it have?

feedback.text: Two counts only the first decision; the second decision at node 4 doubles the maximal paths to four.
Six is the edge count; the maximal simple paths number four.
Recount — combining the choice at node 1 (2 or 3) with the choice at node 4 (5 or 6) gives 2×2 = 4 prime paths.

generalfeedback.text: The graph is acyclic with a branch at node 1 and a branch at node 4, giving four maximal simple paths: 1→2→4→5, 1→2→4→6, 1→3→4→5, 1→3→4→6.

questiontext.text: A CFG has edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 3→4, 4→5, 4→6. How many edge-pairs (length-2 paths u→v→w) does it have?

feedback.text: Four is the number of prime paths; there are six adjacent edge chains.
Recount — node 4 has two out-edges, so each edge into 4 continues two ways, giving six chains.

generalfeedback.text: For each edge u→v, count edges v→w: edges into 4 (2→4, 3→4) each continue via 4→5 and 4→6 (four chains), and 1→2, 1→3 continue into 4 (two chains) — six edge-pairs total.

questiontext.text: How do Edge-Pair Coverage (EPC) and Edge Coverage (EC) compare in strength?

answer.text: EPC is strictly stronger: EPC subsumes EC, but not conversely

feedback.text: Correct — every edge-pair contains its edges, so EPC ⇒ EC, and covering edge-pairs is a stricter demand.

answer.text: EC is stronger than EPC

feedback.text: Backwards — EPC (adjacent edge pairs) is the stronger criterion.

answer.text: They are equivalent on every graph

feedback.text: They differ: covering edges need not cover all adjacent edge combinations.

answer.text: They are incomparable

feedback.text: They are comparable: EPC subsumes EC.

generalfeedback.text: Touring every edge-pair traverses each constituent edge, so EPC subsumes EC; the converse fails because covering edges does not force every adjacent pairing at a branch/merge.

questiontext.text: Which chain lists the structural criteria from strongest to weakest (⊒ means "subsumes")?

answer.text: PPC ⊒ EPC ⊒ EC ⊒ NC

feedback.text: Correct — Prime Path ⊒ Edge-Pair ⊒ Edge ⊒ Node.

answer.text: NC ⊒ EC ⊒ EPC ⊒ PPC

feedback.text: This is reversed; Node Coverage is the weakest, not the strongest.

answer.text: EPC ⊒ PPC ⊒ EC ⊒ NC

feedback.text: PPC is stronger than EPC, so PPC must come first.

answer.text: PPC ⊒ EC ⊒ EPC ⊒ NC

feedback.text: EPC sits between PPC and EC, not below EC.

generalfeedback.text: The structural hierarchy is PPC ⊒ EPC ⊒ EC ⊒ NC; each criterion subsumes the one to its right, and CPC sits above PPC but is usually infeasible.

questiontext.text: A test path tours a prime path with a sidetrip when:

answer.text: It traverses every edge of the prime path in order, but is allowed excursions that leave a node and return to that same node

feedback.text: Correct — a sidetrip preserves all edges of the prime path and returns to the node it departed from.

answer.text: It visits every node of the prime path in order, but may use different edges between them

feedback.text: That describes a detour, which relaxes edges; a sidetrip keeps all the prime path's edges.

answer.text: It tours the prime path with no extra edges at all

feedback.text: That is touring directly; a sidetrip adds an excursion.

answer.text: It skips part of the prime path entirely

feedback.text: A sidetrip never skips the prime path's edges; it adds a return excursion.

generalfeedback.text: Touring with a sidetrip keeps every edge of the prime path (in order) and permits an excursion that leaves and returns to the same node before continuing.

questiontext.text: A test path tours a prime path with a detour when:

answer.text: It visits every node of the prime path in the same order, but may reach the next node via different edges

feedback.text: Correct — a detour preserves the node sequence but relaxes which edges are used.

answer.text: It traverses every edge of the prime path in order, with excursions returning to the same node

feedback.text: That describes a sidetrip, which keeps all edges; a detour only preserves the nodes.

answer.text: It runs the prime path backwards

feedback.text: Order is preserved in a detour; it does not reverse the path.

answer.text: It tours the prime path exactly, edge for edge

feedback.text: That is a direct tour; a detour may substitute edges between the same nodes.

generalfeedback.text: A detour keeps the prime path's node sequence in order but may travel between consecutive nodes by a different route, so it is a weaker touring notion than a sidetrip.

questiontext.text: A test path tours a prime path (directly) when:

answer.text: The prime path appears as a contiguous subpath of the test path

feedback.text: Correct — a direct tour contains the prime path exactly, edge for edge and in order.

answer.text: The test path shares at least one edge with the prime path

feedback.text: Sharing one edge is not enough; the whole prime path must appear contiguously.

answer.text: The test path visits the endpoints of the prime path

feedback.text: Touching the endpoints is insufficient; the entire prime path must be a subpath.

answer.text: The test path has the same length as the prime path

feedback.text: Equal length is irrelevant; touring requires the prime path to be a contiguous subpath.

generalfeedback.text: A test path tours a prime path directly when the prime path is a contiguous subpath of it; sidetrips and detours are relaxed forms used when a direct tour is impossible.

questiontext.text: Why is Complete Path Coverage usually infeasible in practice?

answer.text: A loop creates infinitely many complete paths (one for each number of iterations), so they cannot all be toured

feedback.text: Correct — unbounded iteration makes the set of complete paths infinite.

answer.text: Complete paths are hard to draw in a diagram

feedback.text: The obstacle is their infinite number under loops, not diagramming difficulty.

answer.text: Complete paths are not related to the program's behavior

feedback.text: Complete paths model whole executions; the issue is that loops make them infinite.

answer.text: There is no algorithm to find any complete path

feedback.text: Finding complete paths is straightforward; enumerating all of them is what fails when loops allow unbounded iteration.

generalfeedback.text: With a loop, each iteration count yields a distinct complete path, so CPC would require infinitely many test paths — hence it is generally infeasible, and PPC is used as a practical strongest criterion.

name.text: Count prime paths on a triangle

questiontext.text: A CFG has edges 1→2, 2→3, 1→3 (node 1 initial, node 3 final). How many prime paths does it have?

feedback.text: Correct — 1→2→3 and 1→3 are both maximal simple paths.
Both 1→2→3 and 1→3 are prime; the edge 1→3 is not a subpath of 1→2→3.
Three is the edge count; only two of the simple paths are maximal.
Recount — the maximal simple paths are just 1→2→3 and 1→3.

generalfeedback.text: 1→2→3 cannot be extended, and 1→3 is not contained in 1→2→3 (which lacks the edge 1→3), so both are prime; the count is 2.

name.text: Prime path need not be a test path

questiontext.text: A prime path need not begin at an initial node or end at a final node; a prime path is therefore not necessarily a test path on its own.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — a prime path is a maximal simple path anywhere in the graph; it must be toured by a test path, but it need not itself run entry-to-exit.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Prime paths can start and end at internal nodes (e.g. a round-trip loop), so they are not always test paths.

generalfeedback.text: Prime paths are defined by maximality of simple paths, not by entry/exit endpoints; PPC requires each prime path to be toured by some test path, which does run entry-to-exit.

questiontext.text: Edge-Pair Coverage is defined over paths of length up to 2 rather than exactly 2. Why include the shorter paths?

answer.text: So that edges (and nodes) which cannot be extended into a length-2 path are still required, keeping EPC ⊒ EC ⊒ NC

feedback.text: Correct — the "≤ 2" wording guarantees EPC still subsumes Edge and Node Coverage on small or terminal parts of the graph.

answer.text: Because length-2 paths do not exist in most graphs

feedback.text: Length-2 paths are common; the shorter paths are added for boundary cases, not because pairs are rare.

answer.text: To make EPC equivalent to Prime Path Coverage

feedback.text: EPC remains weaker than PPC; the "≤ 2" wording is about subsuming EC/NC, not matching PPC.

answer.text: To allow paths that repeat nodes

feedback.text: The reason is coverage of non-extendable edges/nodes, not repetition of nodes.

generalfeedback.text: A final node or a graph too small for any edge-pair would otherwise be uncovered; requiring all reachable paths of length ≤ 2 ensures every edge and node is still a requirement, so EPC subsumes EC and NC.

questiontext.text: Prime Path Coverage subsumes Edge-Pair Coverage: any test set that satisfies PPC also satisfies EPC.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — every reachable path of length ≤ 2 is a subpath of some prime path, so touring all prime paths covers all edge-pairs.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Each edge-pair lies on some prime path, so satisfying PPC necessarily satisfies EPC.

generalfeedback.text: Any edge-pair is a simple path of length 2 and hence a subpath of a maximal simple path (a prime path); touring every prime path therefore tours every edge-pair, so PPC ⊒ EPC.

questiontext.text: A CFG has edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→2, 2→4 (node 1 initial, node 4 final). Which listed prime path is a round-trip path (first node = last node)?

feedback.text: Correct — 2→3→2 is a maximal simple path whose first and last node coincide.
1→2→4 is a prime path, but it starts at 1 and ends at 4, so it is not a round trip.
1→2→3 is a prime path but not a round trip (1 ≠ 3).
2→3 is a proper subpath of 2→3→2, so it is not even prime, let alone a round trip.

generalfeedback.text: The loop 2↔3 gives the round-trip prime path 2→3→2 (and also 3→2→3); a round-trip prime path begins and ends at the same node.

name.text: Count edge-pairs with a skip edge

questiontext.text: A CFG has edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→4, 2→4. How many edge-pairs (length-2 paths u→v→w) does it have?

feedback.text: Four is the edge count; only three adjacent edge chains exist.
Recount — node 2 has two out-edges, so 1→2 continues two ways (1→2→3, 1→2→4), plus 2→3→4.
Recount — 1→2→3, 1→2→4, 2→3→4 is three; edges into node 4 have no continuation.

generalfeedback.text: 1→2 continues via 2→3 and 2→4 (two chains), and 2→3 continues via 3→4 (one chain); edges into node 4 cannot continue, so there are 3 edge-pairs.

questiontext.text: Criterion C1 subsumes criterion C2 means:

answer.text: Every test set that satisfies C1 is guaranteed to also satisfy C2

feedback.text: Correct — subsumption is this universal implication between the criteria.

answer.text: C1 and C2 always require the same test paths

feedback.text: That would be equivalence; subsumption is a one-directional guarantee.

answer.text: C1 needs fewer test paths than C2 on every graph

feedback.text: Subsumption is about implication of satisfaction, not about counting test paths.

answer.text: Some test set satisfying C1 also happens to satisfy C2

feedback.text: Subsumption must hold for every satisfying test set, not merely for one.

generalfeedback.text: C1 subsumes C2 iff any test set meeting C1 necessarily meets C2; e.g. PPC subsumes EPC because touring all prime paths tours all edge-pairs.

name.text: Count prime paths with a loop

questiontext.text: A while-loop CFG has edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→2, 2→4 (node 1 initial, node 2 the loop condition, node 3 the body, node 4 final). How many prime paths does it have?

feedback.text: Correct — 1→2→3, 1→2→4, 3→2→4, and the two round-trip prime paths 2→3→2 and 3→2→3.
A common miss: the loop 2↔3 yields TWO round-trip prime paths (2→3→2 and 3→2→3), not one, giving five in total.
Recount — besides 1→2→3, 1→2→4, 3→2→4 there are also 2→3→2 and 3→2→3, so five.
There are exactly five maximal simple paths; 2→3 and 3→2 alone are subpaths, not prime.

generalfeedback.text: The maximal simple paths are: 1→2→3, 1→2→4, 3→2→4, and the two round trips of the loop 2↔3, namely 2→3→2 and 3→2→3 — five prime paths. Rotating a cycle to each start node gives distinct round-trip prime paths.

name.text: Round-trip prime paths of the loop

questiontext.text: For the CFG 1→2, 2→3, 3→2, 2→4, which are its round-trip prime paths (first node = last node)?

feedback.text: Correct — the cycle 2↔3 gives one round-trip prime path per starting node.

answer.text: Only 2→3→2

feedback.text: 3→2→3 is also a maximal simple path with coinciding endpoints, so there are two.
1→2→4 is a prime path but not a round trip (1 ≠ 4); the second round trip is 3→2→3.

answer.text: There are no round-trip prime paths

feedback.text: The loop 2↔3 does produce round-trip prime paths: 2→3→2 and 3→2→3.

generalfeedback.text: Writing the simple cycle 2↔3 starting from each of its nodes gives two distinct round-trip prime paths: 2→3→2 and 3→2→3.

name.text: Count prime paths with a self-loop

questiontext.text: A CFG has edges 1→2, 2→2, 2→3 (node 1 initial, node 3 final; 2→2 is a self-loop). How many prime paths does it have?

feedback.text: Correct — 1→2→3 and the self-loop round trip 2→2.
The self-loop 2→2 is itself a maximal simple (round-trip) path, so with 1→2→3 there are two.
1→2 and 2→3 are proper subpaths of 1→2→3, so they are not prime; the count is two.
Recount — only 1→2→3 and 2→2 are maximal simple paths.

generalfeedback.text: The self-loop 2→2 has first=last=2 with no internal repeat, so it is a round-trip prime path; together with the maximal 1→2→3 that is two prime paths. A self-loop rotates only to itself, so it contributes a single round-trip prime path.

questiontext.text: A prime path is infeasible when no input can drive execution along it. What is the correct consequence for Prime Path Coverage?

answer.text: Literal 100% PPC is unachievable; coverage is measured over the feasible prime paths

feedback.text: Correct — infeasible requirements are set aside so the metric stays meaningful.

answer.text: The whole PPC criterion becomes meaningless and is abandoned

feedback.text: The criterion is kept; only the infeasible prime path is excluded from the target.

answer.text: 100% PPC is still achievable by trying harder

feedback.text: No input can tour an infeasible prime path, so literal full coverage is impossible.

answer.text: The prime path is automatically removed from the graph

feedback.text: The graph is unchanged; the requirement is simply reported as infeasible.

generalfeedback.text: Because no test can tour an infeasible prime path, tools report PPC against the feasible prime paths rather than demanding an impossible 100%.

questiontext.text: A prime path cannot be toured directly by any test path, but it can be toured if a sidetrip or detour is allowed. What is the standard best-effort response?

answer.text: Allow the prime path to be toured with a sidetrip (or detour) rather than dropping the requirement

feedback.text: Correct — permitting sidetrips/detours recovers coverage of prime paths that no direct tour can reach.

answer.text: Immediately declare the prime path infeasible and ignore it

feedback.text: A prime path tourable via a sidetrip is feasible; best effort tours it with the sidetrip instead of discarding it.

answer.text: Delete the prime path from the requirement set with no substitute

feedback.text: Best effort keeps the requirement and satisfies it with a relaxed tour.

answer.text: Require a direct tour anyway, leaving the requirement unmet

feedback.text: If no direct tour exists, insisting on one just leaves the prime path uncovered; sidetrips/detours are the remedy.

generalfeedback.text: When a prime path has no direct tour, best-effort touring permits a sidetrip (all edges kept, with returning excursions) or a detour (nodes kept in order) so the requirement can still be satisfied.

name.text: Why CPC is infeasible but PPC is not

questiontext.text: On a CFG with a loop, why is Complete Path Coverage infeasible while Prime Path Coverage remains achievable?

answer.text: Complete paths are unbounded in number (one per iteration count), but prime paths are simple, so there are only finitely many

feedback.text: Correct — simplicity bounds prime paths; complete paths are unbounded under looping.

answer.text: Prime paths ignore the loop entirely

feedback.text: Prime paths include the loop's round trips; they are just finite because they are simple.

answer.text: Complete paths do not exist when there is a loop

feedback.text: Complete paths certainly exist; the problem is that there are infinitely many.

answer.text: Prime Path Coverage does not require touring the loop

feedback.text: PPC does require touring the loop's round-trip prime paths; it stays finite because prime paths are simple.

generalfeedback.text: A loop lets a complete path iterate any number of times, giving infinitely many complete paths (CPC infeasible); prime paths are simple, so their length is bounded by the node count and their number is finite (PPC achievable).

questiontext.text: How does a prime path differ from a Hamiltonian path?

answer.text: A prime path is a maximal simple path and need not visit every node; a Hamiltonian path must visit every node exactly once

feedback.text: Correct — maximality among simple paths does not force visiting all nodes.

answer.text: They are the same thing

feedback.text: They differ: a prime path can omit nodes, while a Hamiltonian path must include them all.

answer.text: A prime path must visit every node, a Hamiltonian path need not

feedback.text: Backwards — the Hamiltonian path is the one required to visit every node.

answer.text: A prime path must start at the initial node; a Hamiltonian path must not

feedback.text: Neither is defined by the initial node; the distinction is about visiting all nodes.

generalfeedback.text: A prime path is simply a maximal simple path; it may skip nodes. A Hamiltonian path is a stricter global notion requiring every node to be visited exactly once.

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes a prime path from a complete path?

answer.text: A complete path runs entry-to-exit and may repeat nodes; a prime path is a maximal simple path and may start/end at internal nodes

feedback.text: Correct — complete paths are defined by endpoints and allow repeats; prime paths are simple and maximal.

answer.text: Both must run from an initial node to a final node

feedback.text: Only complete paths must; a prime path can begin and end internally (e.g. a round trip).

answer.text: Both forbid any repeated node

feedback.text: Complete paths may repeat nodes (loops); only prime/simple paths forbid internal repeats.

answer.text: A prime path is always longer than any complete path

feedback.text: Complete paths can be arbitrarily long (loops); prime paths are bounded by the node count.

generalfeedback.text: A complete path is any entry-to-exit execution and can repeat nodes through loops; a prime path is a maximal simple path anywhere in the graph and forbids internal repeats.

questiontext.text: A while-loop CFG has edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→2, 2→4. How many edge-pairs (length-2 paths u→v→w, back edges allowed) does it have?

feedback.text: Recount — the back edge 3→2 both continues (3→2→3, 3→2→4) and is continued into (2→3→2), giving five chains.
Recount — 1→2→3, 1→2→4, 2→3→2, 3→2→3, 3→2→4 is five; the edge into node 4 cannot continue.
The loop adds edge-pairs through the back edge (2→3→2, 3→2→3, 3→2→4), raising the total to five.

generalfeedback.text: For each edge u→v find edges v→w: 1→2 gives 1→2→3 and 1→2→4; 2→3 gives 2→3→2; 3→2 gives 3→2→3 and 3→2→4; 2→4 cannot continue. Total = 5 edge-pairs.

questiontext.text: Consider a CFG whose only reachable structure past some point is a single final node with no outgoing edge, so no length-2 path passes through it. Why does the "length ≤ 2" definition of Edge-Pair Coverage matter here?

answer.text: The shorter (length ≤ 1) requirements ensure the incoming edge and the final node are still covered, so EPC keeps subsuming EC and NC

feedback.text: Correct — without the "≤ 2" clause, elements with no edge-pair through them could be missed, breaking subsumption.

answer.text: It lets EPC ignore the final node entirely

feedback.text: The opposite — the clause guarantees the final node is still a requirement.

answer.text: It makes EPC equivalent to Prime Path Coverage there

feedback.text: EPC stays weaker than PPC; the clause is about preserving EC/NC subsumption.

answer.text: It permits paths that repeat the final node

feedback.text: The final node has no out-edge; the clause is about covering non-extendable elements, not repetition.

generalfeedback.text: If a node/edge cannot sit in any length-2 path (e.g. a terminal edge into a final node), requiring only exact length-2 paths would leave it uncovered; the "length ≤ 2" wording adds the shorter requirements so EPC still subsumes EC and NC.

questiontext.text: Which statement about Prime Path Coverage (PPC) and Complete Path Coverage (CPC) is correct?

answer.text: CPC subsumes PPC, but PPC does not subsume CPC

feedback.text: Correct — executing all complete paths tours every feasible prime path, but touring prime paths does not force every complete path.

answer.text: PPC subsumes CPC

feedback.text: Backwards — CPC is the stronger (and usually infeasible) criterion.

answer.text: They are equivalent

feedback.text: They are not: CPC is strictly stronger, requiring all complete paths, not just prime ones.

answer.text: They are incomparable

feedback.text: They are comparable: CPC subsumes PPC.

generalfeedback.text: Every feasible prime path lies on some complete path, so covering all complete paths (CPC) satisfies PPC; the reverse fails because a finite prime-path suite need not exercise every loop-iteration count. Hence CPC ⊒ PPC, and CPC is the strongest but usually infeasible.

questiontext.text: Which pairing correctly states the precise difference between a sidetrip and a detour when touring a prime path q?

answer.text: Sidetrip: every edge of q is traversed in order (with returning excursions). Detour: every node of q is visited in order, but edges between them may differ

feedback.text: Correct — sidetrips preserve edges, detours only preserve the node sequence.

answer.text: Sidetrip preserves the nodes only; detour preserves the edges

feedback.text: Reversed — the sidetrip is the edge-preserving one.

answer.text: Both preserve every edge of q; they differ only in length

feedback.text: Only the sidetrip preserves every edge; the detour may replace edges between the same nodes.

answer.text: Both preserve only the endpoints of q

feedback.text: Sidetrips keep all edges and detours keep all nodes in order; neither keeps only the endpoints.

generalfeedback.text: A sidetrip keeps every edge of q in order and merely inserts excursions that return to the departure node; a detour is weaker, keeping only q's node sequence and allowing different edges between consecutive nodes.

questiontext.text: Which of the following subsumption claims is false?

answer.text: Node Coverage subsumes Edge Coverage

feedback.text: Correct — this is false; NC is weaker than EC, so NC does not subsume EC.

answer.text: Prime Path Coverage subsumes Edge-Pair Coverage

feedback.text: This is true: every edge-pair lies on a prime path.

answer.text: Edge-Pair Coverage subsumes Edge Coverage

feedback.text: This is true: touring edge-pairs traverses each constituent edge.

answer.text: Edge Coverage subsumes Node Coverage

feedback.text: This is true: traversing every edge visits every reachable node.

generalfeedback.text: The hierarchy is PPC ⊒ EPC ⊒ EC ⊒ NC; subsumption points from stronger to weaker, so "NC subsumes EC" is the reversed, false claim.

name.text: Maximum PPC with an infeasible prime path

questiontext.text: A CFG has exactly 5 prime paths, one of which is infeasible. Counting all 5 prime paths, what is the maximum Prime Path Coverage any test suite can achieve?

feedback.text: Correct — the infeasible prime path can never be toured, so at most 4/5 = 80%.
No input can tour the infeasible prime path, so literal 5/5 is impossible.
Coverage is measured over all 5 stated prime paths: 4/5 = 80%, not 3/4.
Only one prime path is infeasible, so up to 4 of 5 are tourable = 80%.

generalfeedback.text: One infeasible prime path caps literal PPC at 4/5 = 80%; in practice coverage is reported over the feasible prime paths instead.

questiontext.text: For the while-loop CFG 1→2, 2→3, 3→2, 2→4, which of the following simple paths is NOT a prime path?

feedback.text: Correct — 2→3 is a proper subpath of 1→2→3 (and of 2→3→2), so it is not maximal and not prime.
3→2→3 is a maximal simple round-trip path, so it is prime.
3→2→4 cannot be extended into a longer simple path, so it is prime.
1→2→3 is maximal (it cannot be extended without repeating node 2), so it is prime.

generalfeedback.text: The prime paths are 1→2→3, 1→2→4, 3→2→4, 2→3→2, 3→2→3; the single edge 2→3 is a proper subpath of longer simple paths, so it is not prime.
